opal.why: Jest's own equality overflows the stack on these values, and opal's expect is Jest's. For nested comparisons, iterableEquality swaps itself for a copy that carries the stack of values already seen, but it filters out only the original, not earlier copies. So the outermost copy, holding a stale stack, is tried first at every depth. An object reached again through a second Set or Map is never found on that stack, and the comparison recurses until the stack overflows. Jest 30.5.2's equals throws the same RangeError on these values; Vitest fixed its copy (vitest#5533).
